title: India Weathered Global Turbulence With Fundamentals Intact, Sitharaman Tells Economists
excerpt: Citing 7.8% Q1 growth, 4.82% August inflation and $766 billion in forex reserves, the finance minister told the Kautilya Economic Conclave that a decade of reforms built India's shock-absorbing capacity.
body:
• India has navigated four years of global shocks with its economic fundamentals intact and strengthening, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said Saturday at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi.
  • Her evidence: 7.8% real GDP growth in Q1 FY27, CPI inflation of 4.82% in August 2026, a current account deficit of 0.5% of GDP, and foreign exchange reserves of about $766 billion.
  • Sitharaman credited a decade of fiscal prudence, infrastructure creation, banking reforms and last-mile delivery — and flagged global public debt nearing 94% of GDP in 2025, projected to hit 100% by 2029, as the key external risk.
  • For investors, the takeaway is policy space: sound public finances give the state room to act when conditions deteriorate, with FY27 capital expenditure budgeted at &rupee;12.22 lakh crore.

India has weathered four years of global turbulence with its economic fundamentals intact and strengthening, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Saturday, crediting a decade of deliberate reform for an economy that absorbed shocks without losing its growth path.

Addressing the special plenary on "Resilience in an Age of Flux: India's Economic Priorities" at the 5th Kautilya Economic Conclave (KEC 2026) in New Delhi, Sitharaman said resilience meant the ability to absorb shocks without losing the growth path while retaining sufficient policy space to respond to future disruptions.

"The evidence of resilience lies largely in the counterfactual, in the outcomes that did not materialise: an inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Union Finance Minister

Context & Background

Sitharaman's address was an accounting of the shocks of the past four years — the West Asia conflicts, energy price volatility, and a tightening global financial environment — measured against India's macro ledger. "Real GDP grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of FY 2026-27. CPI inflation was about 4.8 per cent in August 2026, and the current account deficit was 0.5 per cent of GDP in the first quarter," she said, adding foreign exchange reserves of about $766 billion to the list of buffers.

The contrast she drew was with the rest of the world: global public debt rose to nearly 94 per cent of GDP in 2025 and is projected to reach 100 per cent by 2029 — a level last seen in the aftermath of the Second World War. "A price shock can be cushioned with monetary and fiscal tools. But a quantity shock tests macroeconomic systems, the reach of delivery systems, and therefore the capacity of the state itself. These shocks have arrived in a world with even thinner buffers," she told the gathering. Invoking Kautilya's Arthashastra, she cited the principle "kosha-purvah sarva-arambhah" — all undertakings depend first on the treasury — arguing that sound public finances give the state the freedom to act when conditions deteriorate.

Impact & Analysis

The foundations Sitharaman listed were the post-2014 reform stack: the Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile trinity and Direct Benefit Transfer, PM Awas Yojana, Swachh Bharat, Ujjwala, Ayushman Bharat and food security measures. She noted more than 52 crore collateral-free loans sanctioned under the PM MUDRA Yojana and pointed to banking-sector repair, with non-food credit growing 18.8 per cent in the year to August 2026. On infrastructure, capital expenditure for FY27 was budgeted at &rupee;12.22 lakh crore, with the national highway network expanded about 61 per cent and operational airports more than doubled since 2014.

For global investors, the speech doubles as a positioning statement: the world's fastest-growing large economy is selling macroeconomic predictability at a moment when advanced economies carry historically heavy debt loads. The minister's forward agenda acknowledged the concentration risk, naming strategic resource security, critical minerals, rare earths, semiconductors and small modular reactors as priorities.

Diaspora Angle

The macro numbers travel directly into diaspora portfolios. Sustained 7.8 per cent growth with inflation near 5 per cent and a thin current account deficit is the backdrop behind record NRI interest in Indian equities, real estate and GIFT City instruments. Sitharaman's emphasis on strategic autonomy — reducing single-source dependencies through critical-mineral and semiconductor missions — also signals where state capital will flow next, relevant to diaspora professionals in tech and manufacturing weighing India exposure.

What's Next

"Resilience is not a one-time exercise," Sitharaman said, framing the path to Viksit Bharat by 2047 as continued strengthening of foundations for higher productivity, better employment and wider opportunity. The near-term tests are external: winter energy prices, the West Asia conflict's trajectory, and whether global debt and trade fragmentation tighten financial conditions further. India's answer, per the finance minister, is to keep its powder — fiscal and forex — dry.
